div.head: Hn 75.1
div.ab: Si quis dominum suum occidat, si capiatur, nullo modo se redimat, set decomatione uel e[uiscer]atione uel ita postremo seuera gentium animaduersione dampnetur, ut diris tormentorum cruciatibus et male mortis infortuniis infelicem prius animam exalasse quam finem doloribus excepisse uideatur et, si posset fieri, remissionis amplius apud inferos inuenisse quam in terra reliquisse protestetur.
div.note: New row (October 2026): Liebermann’s text transcribed from Gesetze I p. 591 (two independent readings of the page images, differences settled against the page)

Vgl. Gl Herrenverrat 12; Todesstrafe 6. Zur Schindung vgl. Gl Haut 5. Als der junge Heinrich (III) 1176 Gericht hielt de proditore suo, quidam iudicabant vivum excoriari; G. Henr. ed. Stubbs I 122. Ausweidung (s. d. Gl) kommt in England a. 1242 (Math. Par. Cron. mai. IV 196) und später oft vor (Pol Mai II 499), früher bei anderen Germanen (Grimm DRA 690), so bei Nordleuten auf Irland 1014 (ebd. 520). Ob bei Agsachsen?—Zu decomatio vorher s. Gl Haut 5. Menschenhaut [von Kirchenräubern?] auf Kirchtüren des Mittelalters kennt Pearman Rochester 28.—Schleifen u. Hängen trifft den Herrenmörder nach Très anc. cout. Norm. I 35, 5 und Sel. pleas of the crown 1225 ed. Maitland n. 179; exquisitis tormentorum generibus straft Wilhelm I. heimlichen Mord der Agsachsen an Normannen, wohl oft ihren Herren; Dial. de scacc. I 10—uel eius accusatione{41}—possit{47}—75, 2a do. i.{9} Rs

Cf. Gl Herrenverrat 12; Todesstrafe 6. On flaying cf. Gl Haut 5. When the young Henry (III) held court in 1176 de proditore suo, quidam iudicabant vivum excoriari; G. Henr. ed. Stubbs I 122. Disembowelling (see that word in Gl) occurs in England in 1242 (Math. Par. Cron. mai. IV 196) and often later (Pol Mai II 499), and earlier among other Germanic peoples (Grimm DRA 690), e.g. among the Norsemen in Ireland in 1014 (ibid. 520). Among the Anglo-Saxons?—On decomatio above see Gl Haut 5. Pearman Rochester 28 knows of human skin [of church robbers?] on church doors of the Middle Ages.—Drawing and hanging are the lot of the man who murders his lord according to Très anc. cout. Norm. I 35, 5 and Sel. pleas of the crown 1225 ed. Maitland n. 179; William I punishes the secret murder of Normans by Anglo-Saxons, probably often their lords, exquisitis tormentorum generibus; Dial. de scacc. I 10—uel eius accusatione{41}—possit{47}—75, 2a do. i.{9} Rs
